subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage: Sun, 8:10 pm. Ten days in the new job and I am still fumbling greetings. Today I learned three ways. Yash, the director, put his hand out and gave a firm short handshake, so I did too. A client from the Chennai team put her palms together and I did namaste. A colleague stayed at his desk with a mask on and just nodded, and I nodded back. My mother says a limp handshake looks weak but I noticed that mine was too long today and made someone shift. I am Rashmi and I think the safest approach is: watch what the other person offers, then match. Ask if unsure. It saves some awkwardness.

qa.a: Rashmi has been in the new job for ten days.

qa.q: What might the colleague's mask and nod from the desk have meant to Rashmi?
qa.a: Rashmi took it as a preference to follow, perhaps for health or comfort, though no one could be sure which.

qa.q: What approach does Rashmi settle on?
qa.a: Rashmi decides to watch what the other person offers, match it and ask if unsure.

qa.q: How might Yash have found Rashmi's handshake?
qa.a: Yash probably found it fine, since Rashmi matched the firm short shake, though the long one with someone else made that person shift.

grounding: Diary entry about a young professional choosing a handshake, namaste or nod according to setting and following the other person's lead.

subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage:
Kalyani: Ritu, tomorrow is my first client visit. Handshake or namaste? 😬
Ritu: Watch what they do first. Some people avoid handshakes for health or personal reasons
Kalyani: What if I get it wrong?
Ritu: Then smile and follow. Nobody minds a friendly correction. Keep it brief and firm if it is a handshake
Kalyani: And if it is a man and I am a woman? Some might not shake
Ritu: Exactly. Let them lead. If they offer their hand, take it. If they fold their palms, do the same
Kalyani: Okay. I will also say good morning clearly so it feels warm 🙂
Ritu: Perfect. You will be fine

qa.a: It is tomorrow.

qa.a: Kalyani is anxious about greeting wrongly, shown by the nervous emoji, the "What if I get it wrong?" and the question about gender norms.

qa.q: What advice does Ritu give about greetings?
qa.a: Ritu says to watch what the other person does, let them lead and match it, and keep a handshake brief and firm.

qa.q: How might a client who avoids handshakes feel if Kalyani offered one anyway?
qa.a: The client might feel awkward or pressured, since preferences differ for health or personal reasons.

subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage: Vasudha's first visit to the dairy cooperative at Shirur began with a small puzzle. The secretary, Sumit, came out to meet her with his right arm in a sling. Her hand was already half out for the firm, brief handshake she used at the district office. She stopped it midway, laughed at herself and pressed her palms together instead. "Namaste. I'll spare your arm." Sumit grinned and tipped his head. "Thank you. Fell off the tractor step. Very dignified." Inside, the women from the self-help group sat on a long bench. Vasudha watched first: they were greeting each other with folded hands and nods. She did the same, going down the line. At the end, one young woman, Rupali, stuck out her hand boldly. "Madam, handshake. I learned it at the training in Pune." Vasudha shook it, firm and brief, and Rupali beamed.

qa.q: How did Sumit hurt his arm?
qa.a: He fell off the tractor step.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when she stopped her handshake midway?
qa.a: Vasudha felt a flash of awkwardness and laughed at herself, then was relieved to switch to a namaste that spared Sumit's arm.

qa.q: How did Vasudha choose greetings with the self-help group?
qa.a: She watched first, matched their folded hands and nods, and shook Rupali's hand when Rupali offered it, following each person's lead.

qa.q: How might Rupali have felt when Vasudha shook her hand?
qa.a: Rupali was proud and pleased, beaming because her new skill from the training was welcomed.

grounding: Shows a young professional switching between handshake and namaste according to a health need, local custom and each person's lead.

subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage: On her first client visit in Zurich, Esther had rehearsed the handshake her manager recommended: firm, brief, eye contact, let go. She went round the table: Mrs. Brunner, Mr. Keller, then a young analyst whose grip was barely there. Esther didn't read anything into the soft one; people differ. Then she reached Felix, the project lead, who raised his palm instead and smiled. "Better not. I've got a cold and I'm trying not to share it." For half a second Esther's hand hung in the air, and she felt her cheeks warm. Then she lifted it into a little wave, matching his. "Very kind of you. Hello, Felix." He laughed, and the room relaxed. At the end of the meeting she left him with a nod rather than a hand, and he nodded back.

qa.q: Why did Felix raise his palm instead of shaking hands?
qa.a: He had a cold and was trying not to share it.

qa.q: How did Esther feel when her hand hung in the air?
qa.a: Esther felt a flash of embarrassment, cheeks warming, before seeing that Felix's wave was considerate, not a rejection.

qa.q: How did Esther recover gracefully?
qa.a: She turned the hanging hand into a wave matching his, thanked him lightly, and used a nod at the end, following his lead.

qa.q: How might the young analyst have felt if Esther had judged the soft handshake?
qa.a: The analyst might have felt judged over something that is only a personal style, so Esther's choice not to read into it was fair.

grounding: Shows a young professional using a firm, brief handshake but adjusting to a colleague's health need and different grips by following their lead.

subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage: On his first morning as a physiotherapy assistant at the rehabilitation centre, Jagdish was told two rules: sanitise before touching anyone, and let the patient set the greeting. His first patient, Urmila-ji, a retired schoolteacher, sat on the plinth with her walking frame beside her. Jagdish had his hand half out when he remembered and stepped back to the sanitiser. By the time he turned round, Urmila-ji had pressed her palms together. "Namaste, beta. I don't shake hands with young men. Old habit." Jagdish folded his hands and bowed his head slightly. "Namaste, Urmila-ji. I'm Jagdish. Is it all right if I hold your ankle for the exercises today?" She considered him, then nodded. "That you may." At the end of the session she patted his wrist once. "Good manners. Come again on Thursday."

qa.q: What two rules was Jagdish told on his first morning?
qa.a: Sanitise before touching anyone, and let the patient set the greeting.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when he stepped back to the sanitiser?
qa.a: Jagdish was probably a bit flustered and anxious to get things right on his first morning, catching the rule just in time.

qa.q: Why was asking before holding her ankle wise?
qa.a: It respected Urmila-ji's comfort with touch, especially after she said she doesn't shake hands with young men, so she stayed in control.

qa.q: How did Urmila-ji experience Jagdish's greeting and care?
qa.a: She felt respected, since he matched her namaste and asked before touching, so she trusted him and invited him back.

grounding: Shows a young professional following a patient's lead between handshake and namaste, respecting gender norms and hygiene needs.

subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
passage:
Hi Kiran,
You asked how the first week at the new firm went. Mostly fine, but the greetings nearly finished me.
Monday, the partner gave me a firm, brief handshake, so I matched it: one shake, eye contact, done. Tuesday, a senior lawyer joined her palms in a namaste before I could move, and I did the same. Wednesday, a client, an older man with a bad cold, lifted his hand and said, "No handshakes today, I'm sneezing," so we just nodded. And Thursday, a colleague from the Hyderabad office kept her hands at her sides and smiled, so I put mine on my chest and said, "Good morning."
My one rule now: wait a beat and follow their lead. Nobody minded a pause. They would have minded a grab.
Coffee soon?
Chetan

qa.q: Why did the client say "No handshakes today"?
qa.a: He was sneezing with a bad cold.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel about the greetings during the first week?
qa.a: Chetan felt a bit overwhelmed and unsure at first, joking that the greetings nearly finished the week, but more confident after settling on a rule.

qa.q: What rule did Chetan settle on for greetings?
qa.a: Wait a beat and follow the other person's lead. 👍

qa.q: How might the Thursday colleague have felt if Chetan had reached to shake hands?
qa.a: She might have felt pressured or uncomfortable, since keeping her hands at her sides suggested she preferred no handshake.

grounding: A young professional chooses between a handshake, a namaste and a nod by setting, preference and health, following the other person's lead.
